held_back: The lamp by the victim was left burning, shade turned to the wall
The victim's left shoe was removed and placed neatly by the door
A coin was left on the victim's chest
The clock on the mantel was stopped and turned to face the wall
The front door was locked again from the outside
A glass of water was set beside the body, untouched
Every clock in the house had stopped at exactly 4:12

closers.grudge: Grudges are patient things. They don't need to be fed to stay alive; they only need to be remembered.
closers.money: Money is rarely the reason, whatever the ledger says. It is the thing people reach for when the real reason is too hard to say out loud.
closers.family: The people who know us best are the ones who can hurt us most, because they know exactly where.
closers.silence: A secret is only heavy for the person carrying it. Put it in someone else's hands, and watch how far they will go to take it back.
closers.passion: Jealousy dresses itself up as love for so long that, in the end, even the person wearing it forgets the difference.

unease: Every chair at the table has been pulled out a few inches, as if the house were expecting guests. Four places are laid. {v} lived alone.
The bed is made, and the pillow holds a dent the shape of a head. {v} was found nowhere near it. The sheet is still warm to the back of your hand, which it cannot be.
The family photographs have all been turned to look at the door. Not turned away. Turned to look.
There is a second set of wet footprints on the stairs, going up. None coming down. The upstairs room is empty and the window is painted shut.
The cat will not cross the threshold. It sits in the garden facing the house and watches one window, and does not blink when you wave a hand.
A single line is written in the dust on the mirror, in a child's hand: 'she said it was only for a minute'. Nobody here is a child.
The kitchen clock is running backward, one second at a time. The radio is on, tuned between stations, and under the static someone is counting.
Every door in the house is unlocked and standing open an inch. Every one. Even the cupboards under the stairs.
diaries: The last entries get shorter. 'Things moved again. An inch. Never more than an inch.' Then: 'I stopped checking whether I was imagining it.' Then nothing for nine days. The last line is a single word, underlined twice: 'Patient.'
'Someone has been standing at the end of the garden at night. When I turn the light on there is no one. When I turn it off, there is.' {v} had stopped sleeping in the bedroom a week ago.
{v} had been keeping a list of every time the phone rang and nobody spoke. Forty-one calls. At the bottom, in a steadier hand than the rest: 'They know what time I come home.'
'I have decided not to tell anyone. They would say it is my nerves, and then it would be true.' The entry is dated three days ago. Beneath it, in different ink: 'Good.'
Most pages are shopping lists and weather. Then one page, pressed hard enough to tear: 'It is not what they want from me. It is that they want me to KNOW.'

signatures.text: A single sock, folded, was left on the victim's chest
The nine of clubs was tucked into the victim's collar
Every mirror in the house was draped with a bedsheet
A saucer of milk was set on the doorstep
The victim's hands were folded around one white feather
A paper boat was left floating in the bathtub
The victim's hair was braided with red thread
A key that fits no lock in the house was placed in the victim's palm
A child's crayon drawing of the house was pinned to the door
Every photograph in the house was turned face down
A bar of soap, unwrapped, was set in the victim's hand
The radio was tuned to static and left on low
A ring of salt was poured around the body
An orange peel, in one unbroken spiral, lay on the pillow
A stub of candle was burning in every window
The victim's shoes were lined up on the step, toes pointing at the lake
A single button, not the victim's, was sewn onto their cuff
The kettle was on the boil and two cups were laid out

openers: Little Mercy sits on a ridge above a lake that nobody swims in. It is the kind of town where strangers get waved at, doors go unlocked, and nobody, ever, says goodbye.
There is a particular kind of quiet in a small town after rain. Everyone is home. Everyone is listening. And everyone knows exactly whose light is still on.
In Little Mercy the clocks run a little slow, the gossip runs a little fast, and the lake keeps its own counsel. Nothing happens here. That is what everyone will tell you.
